{

      "category": "perf",
      "title": "Cleanup ticker frequency increased 10x without mention in PR",
      "body": "The cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is a 10x increase in the frequency of background cleanup jobs (including the annotation cleanup and other unrelated cleanup jobs that share this ticker). The PR description and linked issue only describe splitting the annotation cleanup query into two statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks; nothing explains why the global cleanup cadence is being changed. This materially increases database load and lock-contention surface, especially given that the new loop in xorm_store.go will keep running batches back-to-back with no throttle until affected==0. The change should be either justified in the PR description or removed; if it is required to compensate for early termination of `untilDoneOrCancelled` under concurrent activity, that should be stated explicitly."
    },

      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",

      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "doc_defect",
      "title": "Routine cleanup operations logged at Error level",
      "body": "The new code uses `r.log.Error(...)` for routine, expected cleanup activity. After the change, the cleanup path emits six Error-level log lines per batch (`Annotations to clean by time`, `cleaned annotations by time`, `Annotations to clean by count`, `cleaned annotations by count`, `Tags to clean`, `cleaned tags`). Even when the cleanup succeeds these will be logged at Error level and on production systems they will pollute alerting/log dashboards that key off Error severity for `annotation.test`. The success-path log lines should be Debug or Info; only the failure paths warrant Error."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 537,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "doc_defect",
      "title": "'cleaned annotations by time' log message printed even when deleteByIDs fails",
      "body": "The line `r.log.Error(\"cleaned annotations by time\", \"count\", len(ids), \"affected\", x, \"err\", y)` is emitted unconditionally after `deleteByIDs`, including when `y != nil`. Operators reading the log will see a message saying annotations were cleaned alongside an error value, which is contradictory and makes incidents harder to diagnose. The same pattern is repeated on line 557 (`cleaned annotations by count`) and line 579 (`cleaned tags`). The log line should either branch on `err != nil` (different message/level on failure) or use Info/Debug on success and reserve Error for the failure path."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 534,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "doc_defect",
      "title": "Log line always logs a nil error",
      "body": "Immediately before the `deleteByIDs` call, the code logs `\"err\", err` where `err` is the result of `fetchIDs`. Because the surrounding block already returned on `if err != nil { return 0, err }`, the value of `err` here is guaranteed to be nil. The `err` field in the structured log is therefore dead/misleading data and should be removed (or replaced with the result of the delete that follows). The same issue exists on lines 554, 557, 576 and 579."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 607,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "sqliteParameterLimit is wrong: hardcoded 999 instead of 32766 for modern SQLite",
      "body": "The constant `sqliteParameterLimit = 999` is the SQLite compile-time default prior to 3.32, but SQLite >= 3.32 (released 2020) raises the default to 32766, and Grafana's test name explicitly acknowledges this (`should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0`). Because of this constant, any configured batch size between 1000 and 32766 will be incorrectly routed into the unsafe string-concatenation path even though parameterized queries would work. The check should use the higher value (or be looked up via the dialect), and the comparison should ideally be against the actual `len(ids)` rather than the configured batch size — a configured batch of 1000 that returns 5 IDs should still use `?` placeholders."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 609,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "security",
      "title": "String-concatenated SQL with IDs is fragile pattern even though IDs are int64",
      "body": "In the SQLite fast path, the delete statement is built via `fmt.Sprintf(\"DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (%s)\", table, values)` where `values` is constructed by repeatedly formatting `int64` IDs with `%d`. While `%d` on an int64 is safe today, this is a regression from the prior fully-parameterized approach and is fragile: any future change that lets IDs come from a less-trusted source, or that changes the column type, breaks the SQL safety guarantee. The same pattern also bypasses query caching and makes the statement harder to read in slow-query logs. A safer workaround is to chunk the slice into batches of 999 (or 32766) and use placeholders for each chunk."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 585,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "security",
      "title": "fetchIDs interpolates table name unescaped into SQL",
      "body": "`fetchIDs` builds `SELECT id FROM %s` and `DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (...)` with the `table` argument interpolated directly into the SQL string. Today every call passes the hardcoded literal `\"annotation\"` or `\"annotation_tag\"`, so there is no live vulnerability, but the helper accepts a free-form string and there is no whitelist/quoting. A future caller passing user-controlled input (e.g., a table prefix) would create an injection. The function should validate `table` against a fixed allow-list or use the dialect's identifier quoting."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 656,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "data",
      "title": "untilDoneOrCancelled terminates early on any zero-affected batch",
      "body": "`untilDoneOrCancelled` exits when `affected == 0`. With the new two-statement design, an entire batch's IDs can be concurrently deleted (or in the MaxCount case, removed by a concurrent delete on a row that shifts the OFFSET) between `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs`, producing `affected == 0` while there are still annotations to clean. The comment in the code acknowledges the issue for concurrent inserts, but the same hazard exists for concurrent deletes and is more likely. The cleanup will then stop for the current cycle even though rows remain, relying entirely on the (now 1-minute) ticker to retry. A retry that re-issues the same `fetchIDs` (with fresh IDs) instead of terminating would close this gap."
    }

findings.title: Cleanup ticker frequency increased 10x without mention in PR
findings.body: The cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is a 10x increase in the frequency of background cleanup jobs (including the annotation cleanup and other unrelated cleanup jobs that share this ticker). The PR description and linked issue only describe splitting the annotation cleanup query into two statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks; nothing explains why the global cleanup cadence is being changed. This materially increases database load and lock-contention surface, especially given that the new loop in xorm_store.go will keep running batches back-to-back with no throttle until affected==0. The change should be either justified in the PR description or removed; if it is required to compensate for early termination of `untilDoneOrCancelled` under concurrent activity, that should be stated explicitly.

findings.title: Routine cleanup operations logged at Error level
findings.body: The new code uses `r.log.Error(...)` for routine, expected cleanup activity. After the change, the cleanup path emits six Error-level log lines per batch (`Annotations to clean by time`, `cleaned annotations by time`, `Annotations to clean by count`, `cleaned annotations by count`, `Tags to clean`, `cleaned tags`). Even when the cleanup succeeds these will be logged at Error level and on production systems they will pollute alerting/log dashboards that key off Error severity for `annotation.test`. The success-path log lines should be Debug or Info; only the failure paths warrant Error.

findings.title: 'cleaned annotations by time' log message printed even when deleteByIDs fails
findings.body: The line `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y)` is emitted unconditionally after `deleteByIDs`, including when `y != nil`. Operators reading the log will see a message saying annotations were cleaned alongside an error value, which is contradictory and makes incidents harder to diagnose. The same pattern is repeated on line 557 (`cleaned annotations by count`) and line 579 (`cleaned tags`). The log line should either branch on `err != nil` (different message/level on failure) or use Info/Debug on success and reserve Error for the failure path.

findings.title: Log line always logs a nil error
findings.body: Immediately before the `deleteByIDs` call, the code logs `"err", err` where `err` is the result of `fetchIDs`. Because the surrounding block already returned on `if err != nil { return 0, err }`, the value of `err` here is guaranteed to be nil. The `err` field in the structured log is therefore dead/misleading data and should be removed (or replaced with the result of the delete that follows). The same issue exists on lines 554, 557, 576 and 579.

findings.title: sqliteParameterLimit is wrong: hardcoded 999 instead of 32766 for modern SQLite
findings.body: The constant `sqliteParameterLimit = 999` is the SQLite compile-time default prior to 3.32, but SQLite >= 3.32 (released 2020) raises the default to 32766, and Grafana's test name explicitly acknowledges this (`should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0`). Because of this constant, any configured batch size between 1000 and 32766 will be incorrectly routed into the unsafe string-concatenation path even though parameterized queries would work. The check should use the higher value (or be looked up via the dialect), and the comparison should ideally be against the actual `len(ids)` rather than the configured batch size — a configured batch of 1000 that returns 5 IDs should still use `?` placeholders.

findings.title: String-concatenated SQL with IDs is fragile pattern even though IDs are int64
findings.body: In the SQLite fast path, the delete statement is built via `fmt.Sprintf("DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (%s)", table, values)` where `values` is constructed by repeatedly formatting `int64` IDs with `%d`. While `%d` on an int64 is safe today, this is a regression from the prior fully-parameterized approach and is fragile: any future change that lets IDs come from a less-trusted source, or that changes the column type, breaks the SQL safety guarantee. The same pattern also bypasses query caching and makes the statement harder to read in slow-query logs. A safer workaround is to chunk the slice into batches of 999 (or 32766) and use placeholders for each chunk.

findings.title: fetchIDs interpolates table name unescaped into SQL
findings.body: `fetchIDs` builds `SELECT id FROM %s` and `DELETE FROM %s WHERE id IN (...)` with the `table` argument interpolated directly into the SQL string. Today every call passes the hardcoded literal `"annotation"` or `"annotation_tag"`, so there is no live vulnerability, but the helper accepts a free-form string and there is no whitelist/quoting. A future caller passing user-controlled input (e.g., a table prefix) would create an injection. The function should validate `table` against a fixed allow-list or use the dialect's identifier quoting.

findings.title: untilDoneOrCancelled terminates early on any zero-affected batch
findings.body: `untilDoneOrCancelled` exits when `affected == 0`. With the new two-statement design, an entire batch's IDs can be concurrently deleted (or in the MaxCount case, removed by a concurrent delete on a row that shifts the OFFSET) between `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs`, producing `affected == 0` while there are still annotations to clean. The comment in the code acknowledges the issue for concurrent inserts, but the same hazard exists for concurrent deletes and is more likely. The cleanup will then stop for the current cycle even though rows remain, relying entirely on the (now 1-minute) ticker to retry. A retry that re-issues the same `fetchIDs` (with fresh IDs) instead of terminating would close this gap.
